newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels to be offered ransom, asylum - report.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels to be offered ransom, asylum - report.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 72 VIPs may be offered a multi-million dollar ransom, asylum in the Caribbean and the release of some jailed comrades to end the 97-day hostage crisis, a newspaper reported on Monday.

The proposals were drawn up by a commission of guarantors overseeing deadlocked talks between the government and the guerrillas occupying the Japanese ambassador's residence, the daily La Republica said.
The six-point plan to end the hostage crisis will be put to the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas in coming days, the paper said.
Under the secret plan revealed by La Republica, the 20-odd rebels would be paid the money as soon as they walk out of the diplomatic compound they stormed on Dec. 17.

"This payment, of 'several million dollars', would be gathered with the support of the Japanese government and the companies whose representatives are hostages of the MRTA," the newspaper said, quoting a diplomatic source.

Part of this money would be used to distribute provisions to the poor in Lima and Peru's provinces. The newspaper said the government was resisting this point because it would present the MRTA guerrillas as "modern-day Robin Hoods."

The proposals include rebel acceptance of asylum in Cuba and the Dominican Republic; an amnesty for the hostage-takers; improvement of jail conditions for imprisoned MRTA members; and freedom for falsely or harshly-accused MRTA members.

La Republica said the final point could also include the rebel request that U.S woman and alleged MRTA member Lori Berenson, serving a life sentence in Peru on a treason conviction, could complete her sentence in the United States.

Despite the report, there was little indication on Monday that the two sides were nearing agreement. Publicly, the MRTA is demanding the release of some 450 jailed comrades, while President Alberto Fujimori has repeatedly ruled this out.

The three-man mediating commission, which includes representatives from the Vatican, Red Cross and Canada, has been holding separate meetings with both sides since the last round of face-to-face negotiations on March 12.
The hostages include Fujimori's brother Pedro, two Peruvian government ministers, Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki and 23 other Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
